stem:
A 6-year-old who is otherwise well has fever to 39 degrees, cough, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination shows reduced breath sounds and dullness at the right base, and a chest X-ray confirms right lower lobe consolidation without effusion.

What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral azithromycin as the first-line choice
options.explanation: Macrolides are added when Mycoplasma is suspected or as a penicillin-allergy alternative, not first-line for typical lobar pneumonia.

options.label: B
options.text: Oral co-trimoxazole as the empirical agent
options.explanation: Co-trimoxazole is not first-line for typical childhood pneumonia and is used mainly for Pneumocystis in immunocompromised hosts.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Flucloxacillin targets S. aureus, which causes aggressive cavitating pneumonia, uncommon in a well child with simple consolidation.

options.label: D
options.text: High-dose oral amoxicillin as the empirical agent
options.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the dominant cause of lobar pneumonia in school-aged children, and high-dose oral amoxicillin is first-line for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Intravenous cephalosporins are reserved for severe pneumonia, empyema, or failed oral therapy; a well child is treated orally.

context: First-line therapy for uncomplicated paediatric community-acquired pneumonia is amoxicillin, covering Streptococcus pneumoniae. If fever persists beyond 48 hours of treatment, suspect empyema and reassess with ultrasound.
